summary: Identifies common roles of SIP back-to-back user agents, such as IP PBXs, session border controllers and application servers, which go beyond proxies. It is a taxonomy.

plainLanguage.summary: Middlemen who listen to one side and talk to the other. This sorts them into kinds.

questions: what is the difference between a sip proxy and a b2bua
what is a session border controller
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the many kinds of SIP devices that sit in the middle of a call and do more than a proxy.

tldr.problem: Many SIP devices in the signaling path, such as IP PBXs and session border controllers, go beyond what a SIP proxy is allowed to do, yet the only term RFC 3261 gives them is B2BUA.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits B2BUAs into roles by how deeply they act: signaling-plane roles (Proxy-B2BUA, Signaling-only, SDP-Modifying Signaling-only) and signaling/media-plane roles (Media Relay, Media Aware, Media Termination).
tldr.outcome: Other documents can now cite these role names instead of redefining them. It is an informational taxonomy, not a protocol.

today: RFC 7092 is an Informational RFC and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it, so it remains the reference taxonomy of B2BUA roles. It defines no protocol behavior.

sections.title: Why a Taxonomy Is Needed
sections.content:
In real SIP deployments there are many Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs), each with different transparency and purpose. Some act as pure SIP proxies and only become a B2BUA to send a BYE that ends a dead session. Others are full User Agent stacks with application logic joining the server side (UAS) and client side (UAC). Some work only on signaling, while others also touch the media.

As more SIP domains interconnect, a single session is more likely to cross several B2BUAs. The RFC provides names for common roles so other documents can refer to them without redefining them.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a message passing through several helpers, each doing something different. Before we can talk about them, each kind needs a name.

sections.title: What a B2BUA Is, and Is Not
sections.content:
Following RFC 3261, a B2BUA is the logical concatenation of a User Agent Server and a User Agent Client. The classification here describes a role, not a system type. One system can change roles in the middle of a session, for example when a stateful proxy generates BYEs, or when an SBC performs transcoding or REFER termination.

Some things are explicitly not B2BUAs. A typical centralized conference server is the target UAS of many independent UACs, so it is not one. A third-party call control transcoder from RFC 5369 is not one either, whereas an inline conference-bridge transcoder based on RFC 5370 is.
sections.plainLanguage: The name describes what a helper is doing right now, not what kind of box it is. The same box can do different jobs at different times.

sections.title: Signaling Plane Roles
sections.content:
A signaling plane B2BUA works only on SIP messages and headers, not on the media itself. There are three roles.

  • Proxy-B2BUA: looks like an RFC 3261 proxy but keeps enough dialog state to generate its own in-dialog messages, most commonly a BYE. It does not change To, From or Contact, only Via and Record-Route by the usual rules, and it needs to adjust CSeq after generating its own request. It does not inspect MIME bodies, including SDP.
  • Signaling-only: goes beyond proxy behavior even for forwarded requests. It might replace the Contact URI, change or remove Via and Record-Route headers, or modify To and From. No header is guaranteed to be copied across. Examples are an application server that handles REFER locally, or a privacy service proxy doing the header privacy function.
  • SDP-Modifying Signaling-only: also edits SDP bodies, for example removing codecs or merging two media endpoints into one offer, but does not put itself on the media path.
sections.plainLanguage: Some helpers only pass notes along with tiny tweaks. Some rewrite the envelope. Some also change what the note says about how to talk, but none of them carry the actual voice.

sections.title: Signaling and Media Plane Roles
sections.content:
These B2BUAs act on SIP, on SDP and also on media such as RTP and RTCP. A single logical B2BUA may be split into separate signaling and media functions. Three roles are defined, ordered by how deep into the media they reach.

  • Media Relay: ends the media at the IP and transport (UDP/TCP) layers on both sides and copies the payload through untouched. It may police bandwidth or convert between IPv4 and IPv6. It is similar to a NAT and is often the default behavior of SBCs.
  • Media Aware: like a relay, but it inspects and may change the UDP or TCP payload, such as RTP or RTCP, without working at codec level or above. Examples are an SRTP terminator, a device that monitors RTCP for QoS, or one that multiplexes RTP and RTCP on the same 5-tuple.
  • Media Termination: works on the media payload itself, such as codecs or the MSRP message layer. It may only generate DTMF packets, convert between codecs, or act as a back-to-back MSRP agent. Transcoders and RFC 5366 conference servers do this.
sections.plainLanguage: Some helpers also handle the voice. One just passes the sealed package along, one peeks at the label on it, and one opens the package and changes what is inside.

sections.title: Mapping Device Types to Roles
sections.content:
The RFC maps familiar product categories onto the roles. SIP PBXs and softswitches are market terms, not standard ones, and can perform every role depending on architecture or policy. The same holds for Session Border Controllers, though by default most are Media-relay or Media-aware: they replace Contact, remove Via and Record-Route, modify Call-ID, To, From and SDP.

Application Servers are a broad marketing term. Some stay in Proxy-B2BUA or Signaling-only roles, while others, such as IVR or voicemail, are full Media-termination B2BUAs. Transcoders are Media-termination. Conference servers generally are not B2BUAs, except one supporting RFC 5366, which acts as Media-termination when it triggers multiple INVITEs. In 3GPP IMS, the P-CSCF and IBCF with media gateways typically form a Media-relay or Media-aware role, and the S-CSCF typically follows the Proxy-B2BUA role.
sections.plainLanguage: Real products like phone-system boxes and call-security gateways can wear several of these hats. The RFC says which hats they usually wear.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security risks are specific to each B2BUA type. In general, extra systems in the path create extra points of attack, reduce or remove end-to-end encryption, decrease privacy and complicate trust models.

Three general points are made: B2BUA handling of SDP and media impedes end-to-end SRTP and new SRTP key exchange; the ability to modify any header or body affects SIP identity and message integrity; and B2BUA management and configuration interfaces are tempting targets that must be strongly defended.
sections.plainLanguage: Every extra helper in the middle is one more place someone could cheat or peek, so each one needs careful guarding.

viz.caption: B2BUA ROLES FROM SIGNALING ONLY TO MEDIA TERMINATION

layers.label: Proxy-B2BUA
layers.detail: Proxy-like, generates its own in-dialog messages such as BYE

layers.label: Signaling-only
layers.detail: Rewrites SIP headers and some bodies

layers.label: SDP-Modifying Signaling-only
layers.detail: Also edits SDP, stays off the media path

layers.label: Media Relay
layers.detail: Ends media at IP and transport, copies payload

layers.label: Media Aware
layers.detail: Inspects RTP or RTCP, not codecs

layers.label: Media Termination
layers.detail: Works on the media payload, such as codecs
